note: Wednesday 14 Oct 2026, 07:02 SGT -- before Asia's open (SGX 09:00, HKEX 09:30). Tuesday 13 Oct's US cash close is the latest completed session (HKEX/SGX also closed Tue 13 Oct; Korea last closed Mon 12 Oct; Japan's price-spine bar is lagging to Thu 9 Oct in consolidation, not a holiday). Equities closed essentially flat-to-soft (S&P -0.02% to 7,805.45, Nasdaq -0.15%, Russell -0.40%) as mixed Q3 bank earnings (Goldman Sachs beat on trading, JPMorgan a rare miss, Wells Fargo -3%) and a reported one-quarter delay to Nvidia's next-gen Rubin GPU platform offset still-intact AI-capex demand (Google's reported $920M/month multi-year GPU rental deal). Gold/silver stabilized rather than extending Monday's dollar-driven pullback (GLD -0.13%, SLV -1.58%) while oil rallied a third-plus straight session (Brent ~$106, WTI ~$94.7) as the Gulf war widened further -- a tanker and container ship were hit near Hormuz and the Saudi-led coalition struck Houthi fuel depots and intercepted cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh. TODAY'S swing event is the 20:30 SGT US CPI print (consensus: core m/m cooling to 0.2% from 0.3%, headline y/y accelerating to 3.6% from 3.4%), not yet released as of this run; Chair Warsh's first public remarks since the September FOMC come Friday 16 Oct at an IMF fireside chat in Bangkok. Credit stress stays concentrated at the CCC tier (~12.1-12.5% OAS, near its highest percentile on record) while broad HY (3.15%) and BB spreads remain orderly. Rare-earth names (MP, Lynas, UUUU) extended Monday's group-wide selloff into Tuesday with no fresh company-specific catalyst, other than Energy Fuels amending its VAC merger pact to add downside protection against a customer-arbitration dispute -- the Jan 10 2027 China-truce-expiry date remains the operative catalyst window.

macro.regime: Hot-CPI hike-shock meets a widening Gulf War supply premium
macro.narrative: Thursday 15 Oct 2026, 07:02 SGT: markets are digesting a genuinely hotter-than-expected September US CPI print released Wednesday 20:30 SGT -- headline 3.7% y/y (vs 3.6% consensus) and core 2.6% y/y (vs 2.5% consensus), both annualized measures running hot even though the headline m/m matched the 0.6% consensus. Under hawkish Fed Chair Kevin Warsh the print instantly repriced Oct 27-28 FOMC hike odds from roughly 22% to 40-55%, with a December hike now seen as near-certain by several desks; the 10-year Treasury yield spiked intraday toward 5.19-5.33% and the dollar index pushed to an 18-month high near 102.5. That combination hit equities (S&P 500 -1.11% to 7718.94, Nasdaq -1.88%, VIX +10.48% to 16.87) and gold/silver together (SLV -6.11%, GLD -1.49%, silver miners GDX/SILJ/SLVP down 4.4-5.9%) as higher real yields raised the opportunity cost of non-yielding assets -- while oil (Brent +0.17% to $105.87, WTI +0.92% to $95.01) held up on an entirely separate, idiosyncratic Gulf War supply shock (near-daily Hormuz tanker strikes, a Houthi strike on Aramco's Dhahran HQ, Riyadh airport shut through Oct 17) that Goldman Sachs estimates is worth roughly $20/bbl. Two further, unrelated catalysts compounded the tape: China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) unveiling next-gen server DRAM crashed Korea's KOSPI -5.46% Tuesday ('Black Tuesday', Samsung -7.4%, SK Hynix -10%), spilling into chip-adjacent names everywhere including Micron (-4.1%); and Energy Fuels filed a $500M at-the-market share-sale program that knocked UUUU down ~10% to a 52-week low on dilution fears, dragging nuclear/uranium peers (Oklo, NuScale, Centrus) with it even though sell-side ratings on the rare-earth complex stayed broadly bullish. Credit stress remains real but narrow: CCC-and-below HY spreads sit at ~12.1-12.5%, a 4-year high, while broad BB/B high-yield spreads stay calm (~3.15%) -- a genuinely concentrated, not systemic, signal. Breadth was already narrow before Wednesday's drop (only ~43%/29% of S&P names above their 200/50-DMA, McClellan Summation around -1,100), and today's US calendar (Core PPI, Retail Sales, Philly Fed, jobless claims, all 20:30 SGT) is the next test of whether the inflation scare broadens or fades.
